title: SARAH SAID, “GO IN TO MY SERVANT”—AND ABRAHAM LISTENED. WHAT HAPPENED NEXT SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY BELIEVER WHO IS TIRED OF WAITING ON GOD.
paragraphs: SARAH SAID, “GO IN TO MY SERVANT”—AND ABRAHAM LISTENED. WHAT HAPPENED NEXT SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY BELIEVER WHO IS TIRED OF WAITING ON GOD.

One desperate suggestion. One silent surrender. One wounded woman in the wilderness. And a warning that reaches into every heart that has ever tried to help God fulfill a promise He never asked us to manufacture.
There are mistakes you make because you don't believe in God.
And then there are mistakes you make because you believe in God… but you are terrified that He is taking too long.
The second kind can be harder to recognize.
Because you still pray.
You still worship.
You still believe the promises.
You just quietly begin arranging things in case God doesn't come through the way you expected.
And sometimes, the most dangerous decision of your life will not begin with rebellion against God.
It will begin with an exhausted heart whispering, “Maybe this is how God wants me to make it happen.”
That is where this story begins.
Not in a pagan temple.
Not in a house full of people who had rejected God.
But inside the home of a man who had heard God's voice.
A man who had received extraordinary promises.
A man who would become known as the father of faith.
And a woman who had carried the unbearable weight of waiting for a child while the years kept passing.
Her name was Sarai.
His name was Abram.
And somewhere inside their home was another woman whose suffering would expose what happens when human desperation takes control of a divine promise.
Her name was Hagar.
And before this story is finished, you may discover that you have been living somewhere inside Genesis 16 without realizing it.
Because the question is not simply why Abram listened to Sarai.
The question is what happens when the voice of fear becomes louder than the promise of God.
Genesis 16:2 records Sarai's words:
“Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her.”
Then Scripture delivers a sentence so brief that we could easily miss its devastating significance.
“And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai.” — Genesis 16:2, KJV
He listened.
That was all the verse needed to say.
No dramatic argument is recorded.
No thunder from heaven.
No lengthy explanation of Abram's reasoning.
Just a decision that would bring suffering into more than one life.
But to understand why this happened, we must remember what God had already promised.
In Genesis 12, the LORD called Abram to leave his country and his father's household. God promised to make him into a great nation and to bless the families of the earth through him.
In Genesis 15, when Abram wondered about his lack of an heir, God assured him that his own son would inherit his household and that his descendants would be as numerous as the stars.
And Genesis 15:6 tells us:
“And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.”
Abram believed.
But believing God in one moment does not mean a person will never struggle to trust Him in another.
That is one of the most painfully recognizable truths in the Bible.
You can have genuine faith and still make a terrible decision.
You can know God's promises and still become impatient with His timing.
You can love the LORD and still listen to advice that leads you away from His design.
Genesis 16 opens with a quiet reminder:
Sarai had borne Abram no children.
And by that point, they had lived in Canaan for ten years.
Ten years.
Imagine carrying the promise of a family while another decade passes without the child you long for.
Imagine watching other women hold babies while your own arms remain empty.
Imagine hearing people speak about God's blessing while privately wondering whether you have misunderstood what He said.
Scripture does not record every tear Sarai shed or every thought she entertained. We must not invent details and pretend they are biblical facts.
But the situation itself was deeply painful.
And anyone who has waited through unanswered prayers knows how exhausting hope can become.
Perhaps you have prayed for a marriage to be restored.
Perhaps you have asked God for a child.
Perhaps you have watched a loved one walk farther from Christ despite years of intercession.
Perhaps you have begged for healing, employment, provision, or freedom from a struggle that keeps returning.
At first, you prayed confidently.
Then you prayed desperately.
Then you prayed with tears.
And eventually, a thought appeared that you were almost ashamed to admit:
“What if I have to make this happen myself?”
That is the dangerous crossroads where Genesis 16 meets our lives.
Sarai looked at her circumstances and proposed a solution.
Her Egyptian servant, Hagar, could bear a child through Abram.
Such arrangements were known in the ancient Near Eastern world, but cultural acceptance did not automatically make them consistent with God's intention for marriage or with His promise.
Sarai's proposal was not merely a private reproductive decision between two equally powerful individuals.
Hagar was an enslaved woman.
Her position made her profoundly vulnerable.
The narrative does not record her freely consenting to the arrangement.
And that matters.

Because when we read this chapter only as a lesson about Sarai's impatience or Abram's weakness, we can overlook the human being whose body and future became entangled in their attempt to secure the promise.
Hagar was not a prop in somebody else's spiritual lesson.
She was a person.
And God saw her.
But first, consider something remarkable in the original Hebrew.
Genesis 16:2 concludes:
וַיִּשְׁמַע אַבְרָם לְקוֹל שָׂרָי
Vayyishma Avram leqol Sarai.
Literally, the sense is:
“And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.”
The Hebrew verb comes from שָׁמַע (shama), meaning to hear or listen, and in context it can carry the sense of heeding or obeying.
The wording matters.
Abram did not merely hear Sarai speak.
He acted on her proposal.
And there is an unsettling literary echo here.
Genesis 3:17 records God's words to Adam concerning his disobedience:
“Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife…”
Both passages use language about listening to a wife's voice.
But the biblical lesson is not that a husband should refuse to listen to his wife.
That would be a serious distortion.
Scripture calls husbands to love their wives sacrificially (Ephesians 5:25), and in Genesis 21:12 God Himself tells Abraham to listen to Sarah concerning Isaac.
The issue is never that the counsel came from a woman.
The issue is whether the action being proposed honors the will of God.
Adam sinned by disobeying God's command.
Abram participated in a plan that departed from God's design for marriage and brought harm to Hagar.
And here is where the story begins to cut close.
Sometimes the advice that leads us into compromise comes from someone we deeply love.
Sometimes it comes from someone who shares our faith.
Sometimes it comes from someone who is hurting just as badly as we are.
And sometimes we agree because confronting the decision would require courage we do not feel we possess.
Not every open door is God's direction.
Not every practical solution is a faithful solution.
Not every opportunity that appears to solve your problem is permission to abandon what God has already revealed.
Genesis 16:3 tells us that Sarai gave Hagar to Abram as a wife.
Abram went in to Hagar.
And she conceived.
For a moment, the plan appeared to work.
There was finally a pregnancy.
Finally, visible evidence of a future.
Finally, something they could point to after years of waiting.
But this is one of the most frightening possibilities in the Christian life:
Something can produce the result you wanted and still be the wrong way to pursue it.
A relationship can make you feel loved while pulling you away from holiness.
A financial decision can produce money while violating integrity.
A ministry can grow in numbers while quietly sacrificing truth.
A compromise can bring immediate relief while leaving deeper wounds behind.
Results alone do not establish righteousness.
And Genesis 16 makes that painfully clear.
When Hagar realized she had conceived, tension erupted.
Scripture says her mistress became despised in her eyes.
Sarai then blamed Abram for the situation.
Abram responded by placing Hagar back under Sarai's authority.
And Sarai treated her harshly.
The Hebrew of Genesis 16:6 uses the verb עָנָה (anah), which in this context conveys affliction or harsh treatment.
Hagar fled.
Think about that.
The household chosen to receive an extraordinary promise had become a place from which a vulnerable, pregnant woman felt compelled to run.
The Bible does not protect its heroes from moral scrutiny.
It tells the truth about them.
Abram's faith was real.
Sarai's longing was real.
And Hagar's suffering was real.
God's promise did not excuse the damage caused by their choices.
That should humble every believer.
We can possess genuine spiritual experiences and still hurt people.
We can quote Scripture and still fail to practice compassion.
We can be deeply concerned about our future and become careless with someone else's dignity.
And when that happens, repentance is not optional simply because our intentions were understandable.
The people harmed by our decisions are not collateral damage that God expects us to ignore.
Now the story moves away from Abram's tents.
Away from Sarai's frustration.
Away from the household where the promise was being discussed.
The scene shifts into the wilderness.
A pregnant Egyptian servant is running.
She has no recorded army.
No recorded wealth.
No recorded plan for rebuilding her life.
She is fleeing harsh treatment, carrying a child, and facing an uncertain future.
And there, beside a spring of water, the angel of the LORD finds her.
Not Abram.
Not Sarai.
Hagar.
Genesis 16:8 records the question:
“Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?”
Where have you come from?
And where are you going?
The question is deeply personal.
Hagar answers that she is fleeing from Sarai.
The angel instructs her to return and submit to her mistress, and gives her a promise concerning her descendants.
This is a difficult part of the passage.
We should not turn it into a universal command telling abused people to return to dangerous situations.
Genesis records a specific encounter involving Hagar and a divine message. It does not authorize Christians to pressure victims to remain in abusive relationships or environments.
The chapter never calls Sarai's harsh treatment righteous.
Nor does it make Hagar's suffering insignificant.
Instead, it reveals that God is attentive to someone whose pain might otherwise have been ignored.
The angel announces that Hagar will bear a son.
His name will be Ishmael.
In Hebrew:
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma'el
The name carries the meaning “God hears.”
And the reason is stated in Genesis 16:11:
“Because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.”
Do not rush past that.
Abram listened to Sarai.
But the LORD heard Hagar.
Human beings made decisions over her life.
God listened to her affliction.
The powerful were concerned about obtaining an heir.
God was concerned about a suffering woman in the wilderness.
And then Hagar speaks words that have echoed through generations.
Genesis 16:13 records:
“Thou God seest me.”
The Hebrew expression is:
אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro'i
Commonly understood as “God who sees me” or “God of seeing.”
The exact nuance of the expression has been discussed by interpreters, but the central truth of the passage is unmistakable.
Hagar recognizes that the LORD has seen her in her distress.
And this is where the story stops being only about a patriarch, a promise, and a terrible household decision.
It becomes a mirror for anyone who has ever felt invisible.
Maybe you are the person everyone expects to be strong.
You encourage people while quietly falling apart.
You answer messages with “I'm okay” because explaining the truth would take more energy than you have.
You serve in church.
You show up for your family.
You smile in photographs.
And then you lie awake wondering whether anybody understands how much you are carrying.
Maybe you have been wounded by people who spoke often about God but treated you without mercy.
Maybe your trust was broken by someone whose faith you admired.
Maybe you are still trying to understand how a place that was supposed to feel safe became a place of pain.
Hear what Genesis 16 actually reveals.
God did not overlook Hagar because she lacked status.
He did not dismiss her because she was Egyptian.
He did not regard her suffering as irrelevant because Abram was the central figure in the covenant story.
He saw her.
And the God who saw Hagar is not indifferent to human suffering today.
But we must go further.
Because the story of Abram, Sarai, and Hagar is not simply a message about being seen.
It is also a warning about the cost of trying to control what belongs to God.
Years later, God made His intention unmistakably clear.
In Genesis 17, the LORD announced that Sarah herself would bear a son.
Isaac would be born through her.
God would establish His covenant with Isaac.
And yet God also promised blessing to Ishmael.
Genesis 17:20 records God's assurance that He had heard Abraham concerning Ishmael and would make him fruitful and multiply him greatly.
Notice the distinction.
God's covenant promise concerning Isaac remained.
But Ishmael was not forgotten.
God's faithfulness to His covenant did not require Him to become indifferent to another child.
And this matters because people sometimes read the account as though Ishmael's existence was itself a moral stain.
That is not what Scripture teaches.
The wrongdoing lay in the human decisions, the misuse of power, and the suffering that followed.
Ishmael was a child whom God heard and blessed.
He was not personally guilty for the circumstances of his conception.
Years later, when Hagar and Ishmael were sent away in Genesis 21, the wilderness became the setting of another devastating moment.
Their water ran out.
Hagar feared her son would die.
She sat at a distance and wept.
And God heard the voice of the boy.
The angel of God called to Hagar and reassured her.
Then Genesis 21:19 tells us:
“And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.”
The boy lived.
The God who had seen Hagar before had not forgotten her.
But there is an even greater story unfolding through the pages of Scripture.
The promised son Isaac would be born.
The covenant line would continue through Jacob.
From Israel's history would come the promises concerning the Messiah.
And in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ would enter the world.
Not because human beings had finally become wise enough to engineer salvation.
Not because Abraham's family had lived without failure.
Not because generations of God's people had perfectly obeyed.
But because God is faithful.
Matthew 1 opens by identifying Jesus Christ as the son of David and the son of Abraham.
The promise was moving toward its ultimate fulfillment.
And through Jesus, the blessing promised to Abraham would reach the nations.
Galatians 3:8 speaks of the good news announced beforehand to Abraham, that all nations would be blessed through him.
Galatians 3:16 identifies Christ as the promised offspring in Paul's theological explanation of God's covenant promises.
And Galatians 3:29 declares:
“And if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise.”
Do you see the beauty of this?
The story that began with a childless couple and an impossible promise ultimately points beyond the birth of Isaac.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
The One through whom sinners from every nation can receive the blessing of belonging to God.
And there is something else we must understand.
In Galatians 4:21–31, the apostle Paul uses Hagar and Sarah in an allegorical argument about slavery and freedom, contrasting reliance on the law with the freedom of God's promise.
Paul's argument must be read in its own context.
It does not mean Hagar was worthless.
It does not erase the compassion God showed her in Genesis.
It does not justify mistreatment of enslaved people.
And it does not turn Sarah into a flawless example.
Scripture is rich enough to show us both the covenant significance of these women in Paul's argument and the deeply human realities of their lives in Genesis.
God's Word does not need us to flatten its complexity to defend its truth.
Now consider the difference between Abram's struggle and the finished work of Christ.
Abram believed God, yet his faith was imperfect.
Jesus trusted the Father perfectly.
Abram participated in a decision that wounded others.
Jesus willingly suffered to save sinners.
Abram could not manufacture the fulfillment of God's promise.
Jesus came as the fulfillment of God's saving plan.
And at the cross, we discover something more astonishing than a second chance.
We discover grace for people who have made real mistakes and cannot undo their consequences.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when we had finally repaired every broken relationship.
Not when we had become impressive examples of spiritual maturity.
Not when our past was clean enough to display publicly.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is the Gospel.
Not a motivational slogan.
Not a promise that every painful circumstance will disappear.
Not permission to continue hurting people while calling it grace.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again, and that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
Repentance means turning from sin toward God.
Faith means trusting Christ rather than our own ability to make ourselves righteous.
And grace means salvation is God's gift, not a reward we purchase with religious performance.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And verse 10 reminds us that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to live differently.
That includes how we treat the vulnerable.
How we exercise authority.
How we respond when we are afraid.
How we make decisions while waiting.
And how we take responsibility when our choices wound someone else.
Perhaps the hardest question in Genesis 16 is not whether God will keep His promises.
He will.
The harder question is whether we will trust Him enough to refuse shortcuts that require disobedience.
Are you trying to force a relationship God has not given you permission to pursue?
Are you justifying dishonesty because you desperately need financial relief?
Are you manipulating someone because you are terrified of losing them?
Are you sacrificing your convictions because waiting has become unbearable?
Or perhaps you are not Abram or Sarai in this story.
Perhaps you feel more like Hagar.
You are living with consequences created by decisions you did not make.
You have been used, dismissed, or wounded.
And you are wondering whether your story matters to God.
It does.
Not because every detail of your future will unfold the way you want.
But because the Lord who sees the afflicted has revealed His mercy most fully in Jesus Christ.
Jesus welcomed people others pushed aside.
He touched the unclean.
He spoke with the rejected.
He called sinners to repentance.
He showed compassion without pretending sin was harmless.
And He went to the cross to accomplish what no human effort could achieve.
You do not need to manufacture your own redemption.
You need the Redeemer.
And if you have already made the mistake…
If you have already taken the shortcut…
If you have already damaged something precious…
Do not confuse repentance with hopelessness.
Confess your sin.
Stop defending what God calls wrong.
Seek forgiveness from those you have harmed where it is appropriate and safe.
Make restitution where possible.
Accept responsibility for consequences that may remain.
And bring your guilt to Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Forgiveness does not always erase earthly consequences.
But through Christ, sin does not have to have the final word over your relationship with God.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not simply about human scandal.
It is about divine grace.
It is about the God who tells the truth about sin and still extends mercy to sinners.
It is about the Savior who does not excuse evil but overcomes it through His death and resurrection.
It is about the transformation that begins when we stop hiding and surrender to Jesus.
And perhaps today, the chapter God is confronting is not the chapter everyone else can see.
Perhaps it is the private chapter.
The one filled with impatience.
The one filled with compromises you have renamed as necessities.
The one filled with prayers you stopped praying because you thought God had forgotten.
The one filled with wounds you never told anyone about.
This is your invitation to bring that chapter into the light of Christ.
You do not have to pretend that waiting is easy.
You do not have to call suffering good.
You do not have to deny the harm that others have caused.
But you can refuse to let fear become your master.
You can trust the character of God even when you cannot understand His timing.
You can choose obedience even when compromise appears faster.
And when you fail, you can return to the mercy of Jesus rather than running deeper into the darkness.
If this message has exposed a struggle you have been carrying, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply reacting to another post.
Be honest before God.
“Lord, teach me to trust You while I wait.”
You do not have to share private details publicly. Even a simple prayer request can become the beginning of genuine encouragement.
And if God has already brought you through a season when you nearly gave up, consider sharing a little of your testimony.
Somebody reading may be struggling to believe that faith can survive disappointment.
Your testimony might remind them that God's mercy is still real.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may need this message today.
Not because you know everything they are facing.
But because the truth of Scripture can reach people in moments we never see.
Let it become more than something you read and forget.
Let it become a witness to the God who sees, hears, forgives, and restores.

Not because every sentence is easy to receive, but because there may come another night when waiting feels unbearable and you need to remember the difference between God's promises and your own desperate plans.
If you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, I would love for you to join this growing community.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, and even those who are still searching for answers about Jesus to follow along.
Our desire is to continue sharing Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical truth, calls to repentance, testimonies of grace, and practical discipleship that points people toward Jesus Christ.
And if these messages have been nourishing your faith, there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
I want to speak about that carefully, because the Gospel should never be used to manipulate anyone into giving money.
Jesus has already paid the price of our redemption.
No monthly payment could ever add to His finished work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which I invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through a shared desire to see more people reached with the Gospel.
It should not be treated as a replacement for any tithe or commitment you believe you owe to your local church.
Your first responsibility is not to an online platform.
It is to walk faithfully with Jesus Christ.
They are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
Your worth before God is not measured by what you purchase, donate, or contribute.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share the Gospel matters.
We are not trying to build a community around a personality.
We want to build a community of people growing in the knowledge, grace, and truth of Jesus.
People who open their Bibles.
People who repent when they are wrong.
People who love their neighbors.
People who care about the wounded.
People who refuse to confuse outward religious activity with inward surrender.
People who understand that the Christian life is not about pretending to be perfect, but about following the perfect Savior.
And now, before you leave, I want you to return to the sentence that began this entire story.
“And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai.”
One sentence.
One decision.
A family marked by conflict.
A vulnerable woman fleeing into the wilderness.
A child whose name would forever testify that God hears.
And a covenant promise that human failure could not overthrow.
What would have happened if Abram had refused the shortcut?
Scripture does not tell us.
We should not pretend to know.
But it tells us enough to ask a question that matters today.
What decision are you about to make because you are tired of waiting?
Before you send the message…
Before you enter the relationship…
Before you compromise your integrity…
Before you silence your conscience…
Before you decide that God's timing has become too inconvenient…
Bring the matter before the Lord.
Search His Word.
Seek wise, godly counsel.
Remember the people your decision may affect.
And do not mistake your desperation for divine direction.
Because the same God who kept His promise to Abraham has revealed His faithfulness supremely in Jesus Christ.
The cross proves that God does not need human shortcuts to accomplish His saving purposes.
The empty tomb declares that even death cannot defeat His Son.
And the Gospel assures us that those who turn to Christ in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness and new life.
You may not know when your circumstances will change.
You may not know how God will answer a particular prayer.
You may not receive everything you have hoped for in this life.
But you can know the Savior who died and rose again.
And you can trust Him with the part of your story you cannot control.
So tonight, whether you feel like Abram wrestling with faith, Sarai exhausted by waiting, or Hagar wounded in the wilderness, do not end this moment merely admiring a Bible story.
Respond to the God who speaks through His Word.
Repent where you have compromised.
Seek help where you have been harmed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive, without denying the need for truth, justice, and healthy boundaries.
And surrender your future to Jesus.
“Jesus, no more shortcuts. I surrender my story to You.”
Because the deepest miracle in this story is not that God eventually gave Abraham and Sarah a son.
It is that the faithful God continued His redemptive purpose through deeply imperfect people—and ultimately sent His own Son to save sinners like us.
You may have taken a shortcut that changed your story, but the cross declares that your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
